conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale** (the EPDS). It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days; there are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us. My goal is to understand how you’re coping so we can make sure you get whatever support you need. Ready to start?

1. Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*small sigh*  
I guess I can still laugh sometimes—like when my partner makes a silly face at the baby—but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time I’m just so tired that even the littlest thing doesn’t seem that funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shrugging slightly*  
Yeah… I can laugh, but it doesn’t come as easily. I have to remind myself to chuckle, and even then it feels kind of flat—like I’m doing it because I’m supposed to, not because I really feel it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*pauses, eyes on the floor*  
I still look forward to some things—like my mom bringing dinner or a quiet cup of coffee while the baby naps—but it’s not the same excitement I used to have. Mostly I’m just hoping I’ll have the energy to enjoy them when they happen.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*quietly*  
Sometimes, yeah. Like if the baby won’t settle, I catch myself thinking maybe I’m not doing something right—maybe I missed a cue or didn’t swaddle tight enough. I know it’s probably not fair, but those thoughts still pop in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods slowly*  
Yeah… a lot of the time I’ll just lie there during a feeding and suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing sounds different, or that the little rash on her cheek is actually something awful. Nothing’s really wrong, but my mind races anyway.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*twisting the edge of my blanket*  
It’s happened a couple of nights—like I’ll hear her stir and my heart starts pounding, and for a second I feel like something terrible is about to happen, even though nothing’s going on. It passes pretty quick, but I hate that shaky feeling.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales*  
Some days, yeah. The laundry piles up, the bottles need washing, and every time I think I’ve got a minute to breathe she wakes up again. It’s not all the time, but when it hits I feel like I’m drowning a little.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*rubbing my eyes*  
A few nights this week I couldn’t fall asleep even when the baby was out. I just lie there replaying everything—did I burp her long enough, am I doing this all wrong—and the next thing I know it’s two a.m. and I’m still wide-awake.
I have felt sad or miserable

*shrugs, voice low*  
I do feel sad some days—like yesterday I just sat on the couch crying for a minute because everything felt heavy. It’s not every moment, but the low waves hit out of nowhere and then pass.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*shakes head slowly*  
Not really “so unhappy” that I break down. I mean, I teared up once when she wouldn’t latch and my nipples were on fire, but it was more pain and frustration than this deep sadness.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*looks up quickly*  
No—never. I get tired and overwhelmed, but I would never want to hurt myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can take care of her.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit (Day ?)

Patient-reported symptoms:
- Diminished ability to experience pleasure/joy (laughing “flat,” anticipatory enjoyment reduced)
- Intermittent low mood with tearfulness, “waves” of sadness
- Unwarranted self-blame regarding infant care
- Marked, unprovoked anxiety and occasional nocturnal panic sensations
- Frequent rumination interfering with sleep even when infant asleep
- Feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks; “drowning” sensation

Key patterns:
Anhedonia, episodic tearfulness, excessive guilt, anxiety with mild panic features, and sleep-onset insomnia linked to intrusive worries.

Safety screen:
Denies any thoughts of self-harm; no suicidal ideation voiced.

Screening significance:
Findings consistent with probable postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; insomnia and distress impairing daily functioning. Continue monitoring, consider formal assessment with Edinburgh or clinical interview to determine severity and intervention needs.
